gloss: tree radical (木); the left-hand "tree" radical in kanji

definitions.gloss: tree radical (木); the left-hand "tree" radical in kanji
definitions.explanation: The kanji radical {木|き}, the {偏|へん} (left-side) form of the character for tree. It appears in many kanji related to trees, wood, and wooden objects, such as {林|はやし}, {森|もり}, {村|むら}, {机|つくえ}, {板|いた}, and {柱|はしら}.

examples.japanese: 「{林|はやし}」はきへんの{漢字|かんじ}だ。
examples.english: "林" is a kanji with the tree radical.

examples.japanese: きへんの{漢字|かんじ}は{木|き}に{関係|かんけい}することが{多|おお}い。
examples.english: Kanji with the tree radical often relate to trees or wood.

examples.japanese: 「{村|むら}」はきへんに{寸|すん}と{書|か}く。
examples.english: "村" is written with the tree radical plus 寸.

examples.japanese: {名前|なまえ}の「{柏|かしわ}」は、きへんに{白|はく}と{書|か}きます。
examples.english: The name "柏" is written as the tree radical plus 白.

notes:
The name literally means "{木|き}-{偏|へん}" (tree-left-side-radical). Like other radical names, きへん is usually written in hiragana when cited or described in speech.

USAGE:
Native speakers routinely use radical names to describe kanji verbally — for example, when giving a rare surname over the phone or clarifying a character: きへんに{白|はく}で「{柏|かしわ}」. This is a standard conversational tool for disambiguation.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- きへんの{漢字|かんじ}: a kanji with the tree radical
- きへんに〜: tree radical next to 〜 (used when spelling out kanji)
- きへんが{付|つ}く: to have the tree radical attached

KANJI WITH THIS RADICAL:
Common examples include {林|はやし} (woods), {森|もり} (forest), {村|むら} (village), {机|つくえ} (desk), {板|いた} (board), {柱|はしら} (pillar), {橋|はし} (bridge), {松|まつ} (pine), and many more.

SIMILAR WORDS:
- にんべん: person radical ({亻|にんべん}), another common left-side radical
- さんずい: three-drops-of-water radical ({氵|さんずい}), used in water-related kanji
- {偏|へん}: the general term for left-side radicals
- {部首|ぶしゅ}: radical (general term for kanji components)
